title: Money that stops moving: cash and investments that pile up
question: Which organizations kept adding to their cash and investments year after year while City payments continued, and which that live mostly on City money hold the most in reserve?
finding: The middle organization among 466 with full returns held 4.6 months of spending in cash and investments at its latest year-end; the middle one among the 120 that get half or more of their revenue from the City held 2.3 months. 28 organizations with at least a quarter of revenue from the City added to reserves in each of the last three years or more, by $56.3 million in total while the City paid them $342.8 million; the largest rise is Community Youth Center San Francisco, from $7.2 million to $15.8 million. 29 mostly City-funded organizations held six months of spending or more, 8 of them a year or more; the largest reserve in that group is Self-Help For The Elderly with $20.0 million, 7.2 months of spending.
how: Reserves are cash, savings and temporary investments, and publicly traded securities at year-end on the balance sheet of the return (Part X lines 1, 2 and 11). Months of spending is reserves divided by one-twelfth of the year's total expenses. "Grew every year" needs at least four consecutive year-ends, each higher than the last, ending at the latest return, a rise of $250,000 or more, City payments of $100,000 or more in each of those years, and City money equal to a quarter or more of revenue in the latest year. "Mostly City-funded" means City payments in the latest tax year were half or more of total revenue and at least $250,000; those holding six months or more, and spending at least $250,000 a year, are listed. The cents column is the rise in reserves for every dollar the City paid over the same years. City share of revenue is shown as 100% where City payments exceed reported revenue.
limits: A reserve is not idle money by definition. It may be restricted by donors, set aside for a building, held for other organizations, or received in advance for work not yet done; the note column says where the return shows one of these. Holding several months of spending is ordinary prudence, and an organization that is reimbursed after the work is done needs cash to meet payroll while it waits. Reserves built from private gifts are the organization's own affair. The comparison does not show that City money, rather than other income, is what accumulated. Other investments and property are left out, so true reserves can be higher. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. For 23 of the 485 organizations matched here that makes the City figure at least $1 million and 10% higher over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $1.36 billion higher in all. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. A return may not count money that passes through as revenue. For the organizations matched here, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $425.1 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (14 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
